title: Gilcrest Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Gilcrest wells have a 50 ft median depth, 15 gpm median reported yield, and completed-well costs of $8,500-$15,500.
h1: What Gilcrest Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Gilcrest sits on the Weld County plains, where the well records point to relatively shallow drilling and strong reported yields. Within five miles of town, Colorado DWR records show 2,946 permitted wells, including 1,876 recorded as constructed.

The numbers are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for one parcel. A well permit, neighboring completion reports, the aquifer listed on the permit, and an on-site driller's evaluation all matter before you buy land or price a build.

sections.heading: Gilcrest well depths are usually shallow
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Gilcrest is 50 feet. The middle half runs from 22 to 70 feet, so a driller bidding a typical residential well may be working in that general range rather than automatically planning a deep hole. The 90th-percentile depth is 105 feet.

Depths are not uniform. About 88% of reported wells are under 100 feet, while 7% fall between 100 and 300 feet and 5% between 300 and 600 feet. The deepest record reaches 568 feet. Permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers most often, with 1,791 wells, while 566 name the Alluvial aquifer and 125 name Laramie Fox Hills. That mix is a reason to check nearby logs instead of relying only on the town-wide median.

sections.heading: Reported Gilcrest yields are generally strong
sections.html:
Among the 391 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is listed from 14.2 to 750.0 gallons per minute, a very wide spread that tells you the local records are not all measuring the same practical water situation in the same way.

Three quarters of reported wells show yields of 15 gallons per minute or more. Another 23% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 2% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute. A strong reported yield still does not promise that a new hole will match it, so ask for the pumping-test method, recovery information, storage capacity, and the full completion report before treating a yield number as dependable household supply.

sections.heading: The Gilcrest water table appears closer to the surface
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from the ground surface to water in a well when it is not being pumped. The local median is 11 feet, with the middle half between 6 and 19 feet. That is shallow enough to affect drilling, casing, trenching, and construction planning.

The decade series does not suggest a dropping water table in these records. The median measured depth to water was 18 feet in the 1960s, 12 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet in the 2020s. These are measurements from different wells and locations, not a controlled monitoring network, so they should not be read as proof that groundwater is rising everywhere. Seasonal conditions, well construction, pumping, and the mix of measurement sites can change the comparison.

sections.heading: Gilcrest permit history shows steady recent activity
sections.html:
Permit records go back to the 1950s, with 142 permits issued in that decade and 226 in the 1960s. Activity was lower in the 1970s and 1980s, then increased to 353 permits in the 1990s and 348 in the 2000s. There were 278 permits in the 2010s and 579 in the 2020s. The newest permit year in the records is 2026.

The most active names in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 707 wells, Clement, Glenn A., with 193, and R & R Well & Pump Inc. (Rank, Samuel C), with 90. These are record associations, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, availability, insurance, scope of work, and who will handle the permit and pump installation.

sections.heading: A typical Gilcrest well budget starts shallow
sections.html:
The cost model for Gilcrest uses a typical drilling rate of $50-$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole alone models to about $2,500-$3,500. That is the excavation and drilling portion, not the finished water system.

Including a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, the modeled finished-well cost is about $8,500-$15,500. A shallow median does not eliminate cost differences: access, casing and grout requirements, water-system layout, power distance, difficult ground, testing, and site conditions can move the bid. Request a written scope that separates drilling from casing, development, pump work, tank, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
Well quantity is only one part of due diligence. Mapped environmental data within about 10 miles includes 2,506 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped sites do not prove contamination at a particular lot, but they are a clear reason to test existing water and obtain site-specific guidance before closing.

Only 213 wells report a static water level and 391 report a pump yield, so the available performance data cover a fraction of the records. Fractured or variable formations can produce different results on adjacent parcels, including a low-yield or dry hole. Confirm septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, well-to-septic separation, building envelopes, access for a rig, and the final location of the house, driveway, and utility trenches before drilling.

sections.heading: Use nearby records before buying a Gilcrest lot
sections.html:
Start with the closest comparable wells, not the broadest statistic. Look around Gilcrest and nearby Milliken, Evans, Platteville, La Salle, Johnstown, and Greeley for construction depth, aquifer name, yield, static water level, use, and permit age. A neighboring 50-foot well can be informative, but it is not a promise for your parcel.

Ask the seller for the well permit, construction report, pump information, water tests, and any records of shortage or repairs. Domestic and household wells make up 25% of the local use mix, while irrigation accounts for 28%, monitoring 31%, and stock 9%; that means a high-yield irrigation record may not represent a household installation. If you are building, have a Colorado driller and septic professional review the lot together, then price the complete water system rather than drilling alone.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Gilcrest?
faq.a: The median reported depth within five miles of Gilcrest is 50 feet, and the middle half runs from 22 to 70 feet. About 88% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Some are much deeper: 7% are between 100 and 300 feet, 5% are between 300 and 600 feet, and the deepest record is 568 feet.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Gilcrest?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 50-foot median depth, drilling the hole models to about $2,500-$3,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $8,500-$15,500. Access, casing, grout, testing, utilities, and site conditions can change the actual bid.

faq.q: How much water do Gilcrest wells produce?
faq.a: Of the local wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 14.2 to 750.0 gallons per minute. About 75% report 15 gallons per minute or more, while 23% report 5-15 gallons per minute. These results are not a guarantee for a new well, so review nearby tests and completion reports.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Gilcrest?
faq.a: A local well should be tested rather than assumed safe. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 2,506 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those maps do not establish contamination on your lot. Test existing water, review the well location and history, and use qualified local guidance for the testing plan.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Gilcrest?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a dropping trend. Median depth to static water was 18 feet in the 1960s, 12 feet in the 2010s, and 8 feet in the 2020s. The comparison uses different wells and measurement sites, however, so it is not proof of a uniform groundwater rise. Seasonal pumping and well conditions can affect the results.
